topics.title: Workout Programming Considerations
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/Academy - Programming and Progression 1 - Workout Programming Considerations.txt
topics.moduleLabel: General Recommendations for Programming and Progression

blocks.text: As mentioned throughout this manual, most clients/trainees will benefit from the exact same or similar programming. This is because physiologically speaking, the human body is essentially the same across the species. Aside from limb length differences, postural asymmetries, and slight variations in muscle attachment locations (creating differing internal moment arms), our muscular architecture is remarkably similar. Especially when considered for purposes of effective resistance training.

Because of this, most trainees will benefit from a basic foundational program that is known as a "generic" routine or "the big 5". This program consists of a horizontal push and pull (so chest press and compound row), a vertical push and pull (overhead press and pulldown), and a leg press. These five exercises alone will target (and therefore stimulate) most of the major muscular structures of the body, especially for newer trainees. As a subject gets more advanced, a more specialized selection of targeted exercises should be considered including single joint or unilateral movements. And as discussed below, subjects with certain orthopedic issues will benefit from other, more specific exercises.
Where to Begin...?

Most clients will be introduced to the Leg Press and at least one other exercise during the consultation. The other exercise will most likely be an upper body pulling movement (preferably compound row). These exercises are selected for their relative simplicity to learn and they address a multitude of muscular structures because of their compound nature. Keep in mind, compound exercises are linear movement patterns that act on more than one joint in the body.

In special cases, a new client that has a problematic or compromised joint or area of the body may alternatively be introduced to a more targeted exercise. For instance, someone with lower back issues may be given the lumbar machine during the consultation to highlight the therapeutic nature of resistance training and our protocol. It should go without saying that in this situation the instructor must be cautious in selecting the resistance and range of motion to ensure the safety of our clients, which is really what is expected in all situations at MSF.

After the client has completed their consultation and they return for their first workout, there's not necessarily a "best" course of action. The most sensible balance we should be seeking in a program would begin with selecting exercises from basic categories. The following table illustrates these basic categories and the exercises that are included in each:

From the highest, most broadly considered perspective, a client with a clear medical history and the goal of being functionally stronger would probably be best to eventually have an exercise from each category in a given workout. Or at least have each category represented through the weekly or rotational volume. So for instance if the client has been with us for several months and has an A and B rotation of workouts, each category would be represented at least once across both workouts with the first three categories most likely appearing in each workout. The first three categories (upper body - pull, upper body - push, and legs) can be seen as foundational and containing the "generic" routine exercises discussed above. For this reason, these three categories should most likely be included in every workout with the balance of exercises coming from the trunk and/or hip categories as needed for each specific client situation.
Case Study Examples:

A 65 year old client with a knee replacement and knee pain looking to remain as active as possible as they age. In this situation, we would definitely consider including a combination of the leg curl, along with leg press or leg extension in a majority if not all of the workouts. They would also most certainly benefit from hip and lumbar exercises as these tend to be areas of concern for the aging population. The remainder of the program would be comprised of the upper body push and pull exercises. This would constitute a well rounded, full body program that addresses the client's major concerns.

A 55 year old golf enthusiast with back pain looking to continue golfing as long as possible. As we have now learned a stronger golfer is a better golfer, just as a stronger gardener is a better gardener. That is to say the general quality of strength makes one better (i.e. more efficient or more capable) at anything. So in this case, we simply want to make the client generally stronger with a program that includes upper/lower push and pull along with lower body exercises. But more specifically in this case, the client would most likely benefit from a focused attention to their spine and core. Consider rotating between lumbar, abdominal, and torso rotation to better develop balanced strength in muscles that have been asymmetrically used in their sport/hobby.

An ectomorphic (lean/slender) 30 year old looking to be more muscular. In this case, this client might be better served to perform the "generic" or "big 5" routine for as long as possible. As discussed above, this program targets the most muscle over each of the five movement patterns. After some time, the instructor may add in the lateral raise and some direct, single joint arm exercises. Someone looking to be generally more muscular wouldn't necessarily benefit from more functional exercises such as hip abd/add or lumbar, at least from an aesthetic perspective. That is not to say that these movements should never be included, eventually they should. But if we're looking to deliver results in this situation, then the exercises described will lead to the most favorable results. And in this situation, we're not doing a disservice by not including the other exercises as the exercises we are performing will build overall, general strength.

A 78 year old grand parent with hip pain and balance concerns that wants to keep up with their grandchildren. Again, building general strength is going to help this individual the most so we will include exercises from the first three categories without question. But with balance concerns and their given age, there should be a consideration to include a consistent regimen of hip exercises, both abd and add, along with strengthening the core with lumbar and abdominal exercises.

A 40 year old recently recovering from a shoulder surgery. In this case, there may be a contraindication to performing any upper body exercises at all. As exercise practitioners we need to inform our clients that they can still train the other muscles of the body if they have an injury or are recovering from a surgical procedure. So for this client, we would just perform all lower body exercises to at least keep that area strong. There are not many situations that would keep a client away from their workouts with us for any extended period of time.

topics.title: Novice Level Trainees
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/Academy - Programming and Progression 2 - Novice Level Trainees.txt
topics.moduleLabel: General Recommendations for Programming and Progression

blocks.text: The first session or consultation is where we present the Preliminary Considerations and introduce the leg press and one other additional exercise, usually overhead press or compound row.
Refer to the leg press script for the introduction of the MSF Protocol to the subject.
Once the subject has been introduced to the leg press it becomes easier to learn a compound upper body exercise (or any exercise for that matter).

During the client’s second session, a third exercise will be added and these three exercises MAY be performed twice to help speed up the learning curve, depending on the clients proficiency. If they are slow to grasp the concepts or intensity adverse, it may help to perform the exercises twice in the initial workout or two. If they are quick learners, the trainer may add a fourth and fifth exercise and only perform one set of each. Of course these single sets will be closer to a maximum effort and thus the reason for only performing one set (i.e. our protocol). If the overhead press was introduced during the consultation, the compound row would usually be the exercise added for the second workout.
This four/five-exercise workout may be repeated for several subsequent sessions if the instructor determines it necessary to engrain the basic qualitative concepts.

Beginners are allowed and expected to have a higher rep count (8 to 12) as the weights should be light enough to facilitate learning. They need to be able to exaggerate their control on every exercise. Especially the changes of direction. This takes a lifetime to master so we may start with a somewhat lighter load to begin to learn the control required.
For this reason, the beginner workout will likely be longer than an intermediate or advanced level workout, lasting upwards of 30 minutes.

If the subject appears to be grasping the fundamentals accordingly, the instructor can begin to build their A routine over the next few workouts and ultimately introducing exercises for the B routine.

topics.title: Intermediate Level Trainees
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/Academy - Programming and Progression 3 - Intermediate Level Trainees.txt
topics.moduleLabel: General Recommendations for Programming and Progression

blocks.text: At a certain point of mastery of the basics, the instructor will determine that the subject is ready to learn new exercises beyond the A routine. For a majority of subjects and based on individual proficiency, the basic A routine should be performed no less than 5 to 7 times before beginning to add new exercises. To rush into additional exercises almost always shifts the focus away from mastering the movement and control in general.

Adding exercises must be done in a planned fashion so as not to introduce or include too many at once. Therefore, a second routine (B routine) needs to be created over time. This will take place over the course of several or more workouts where the new exercises are added to some of the A routine exercises (usually replacing one at a time). Again, our focus needs to be on the quality of the effort not the number of exercises. So take time to spread this out for several or more weeks if you can. Eventually, there will be enough new exercises introduced and learned to be able to create two separate routines (the original A routine and the newer B routine).

New exercises should be introduced and programmed for several consecutive sessions to help speed up the learning curve. Remind the subject that the new exercises may not be performed as intensely for purposes of proper learning and we will progress accordingly. Give positive feedback if they seem to grasp the movement quickly and then make sure to consider using a challenging load on the next session. But first they must pass our high standards. Perform the movement perfectly. Especially the changes of direction.
Intermediate subjects will typically have shorter set durations than that of a beginner as the loads used will have increased commensurate with proficiency (expect somewhere between 5 to 10 reps).

topics.title: Advanced Level Trainees
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/Academy - Programming and Progression 4 - Advanced Level Trainees.txt
topics.moduleLabel: General Recommendations for Programming and Progression

blocks.text: As a client progresses to an advanced level, the instructor may determine to introduce more exercises and begin to build a C routine. And remember, having more exercises isn't necessarily a better workout or program. The Big 5 are plenty and can provide profound benefit for a lifetime. So a C isn't better, or required, or to even be aspired to. It should happen out of necessity and time. And importantly, it should be slowly introduced, one movement at a time, similar to the B routine. Additionally, once the C routine has been fully introduced it should be run consistently for at least 2 consecutive workouts before rotating between A, B, and C. Again, this is to facilitate proficient learning of the exercises with emphasis on mastering the protocol.

Advanced level subjects may have set durations as low as 3 reps but this is rare. The upper limit should not go above 9 reps in most cases as this would equate to a 3-minute set and would begin to fall outside of the constraints of a high-intensity effort.

In summary, clients should remain on the basic A routine for as long as possible. Progressing to new routines should only be considered when absolutely necessary and after the subject has shown proficient mastery of the protocol.

blocks.text: Instructors will frequently field questions from clients regarding plateaus in exercise progression. As most exercise enthusiasts realize, progression has a limit but almost no one has yet completely reached it when you take into account the following considerations.

At the outset of the MaxStrength Fitness program, an increase in weight or repetitions or both should be expected. But it is important that the instructor be able to have ongoing intelligent and informative discussions with a client that these factors cannot and will not continue forever. And that the qualitative elements of the workout should be the singular focus as this practice will lead to deeper levels of fatigue and a more meaningful stimulus.
The following factors should be considered for workout progression and are listed in order from the highest priority to the lowest priority:
Form – the quality of execution of the rep/set is the most important factor to improve upon before anything else in the workout is considered.
Sequence of exercises - needs to follow a logical order where there are no conflicting movement patterns and complementary pairings are considered:
Conflicting Movement Patterns:

Lumbar and Leg Press should NOT be run contiguously in any arrangement. The fatigue from the Lumbar exercise will interfere with the execution of the LP. LP requires a certain amount of trunk flexion and there will likely be some discomfort experienced from having worked the low back immediately before. At the same time, performing the LP immediately before Lumbar will cause some discomfort from locking down the legs and pelvis.
Lumbar into Leg Curl should be avoided as the fatigue from the Lumbar movement will only be increased by the trunk extension required of the LC.

Repetition count – if a subject has yet to reach muscular fatigue/failure and is still within an acceptable rep count range, the number of reps should be progressed in an effort to approach failure, before resistance is added.
Resistance – weight increases are only considered after the previous four factors are optimized

topics.title: AB Routines - How to Optimize Programming
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/Programming and Progression 6 - AB Routines - How to Optimize Programming.txt

blocks.text: When considering an optimal A/B routine for the general population, we must first remind ourselves that hypertrophy is muscle fiber specific. Meaning only those muscle fibers recruited/activated by an exercise will benefit from a training stimulus. In other words, if we are implementing a full body program, then an individual workout should target as many muscle fibers (i.e. muscle groups) as possible.

The next critical consideration to make is that long-term hypertrophy is only accomplished with an at least twice per week stimulus (i.e. minimum effective dose). This, in connection with the fact that hypertrophy is muscle fiber specific, means that similar muscle fibers/regions must be stimulated twice per week. If we program with “too much” variety, we will dilute the required frequency. For instance, if we target the pecs directly in an A routine but then neglect them in the B routine, the net effect will be that we are only truly targeting those fibers once per week. While this may be enough to ensure strength gains over time, it will likely fall short in terms of continually building muscle beyond a certain level of development.
Importantly, strength is not an adaptation itself but rather an outcome of the following six adaptations:
Improved coordination
Increased Motor Unit Recruitment (MUR)
Decreased antagonist coactivation
Hypertrophy
Increased tendon stiffness
Lateral force transmission

You’ll note that one of the adaptations of strength is the increase in muscle tissue, or hypertrophy. Hypertrophy is its own adaptation and it contributes to the outcome that is increased strength. While most of the adaptations that underpin strength are more easily achieved and with less frequency (especially the first three CNS adaptations), hypertrophy requires a twice per week stimulus over the long term. Importantly, muscle tissue will absolutely be built with a once per week frequency, especially in a more novice subject, but the most optimal approach is to target the same muscle fibers more frequently.

In considering the points outlined above, the ideal training program would consist of as many exercises as can be recovered from that target as many muscle fibers as possible. And this program would repeat with zero variation, indefinitely. But this approach is not realistic as most clients will expect and appreciate variety. Unfortunately, people are too easily “bored” with exercise programs even if they would produce better long-term results. Because of this, we must find ways to be creative with our programming to accomplish the following:
Coverage of the desired target areas (most will be full body)
Variety to satisfy/motivate the client
Consistency of the stimulus (frequency of similar muscle regions)

One last concept to be aware of before presenting an optimal A/B routine is what’s known as regional hypertrophy. Essentially, with regional hypertrophy, there is an additive benefit for novice trainees due to their lack of muscular development. This benefit allows more muscle regions to be stimulated from a given exercise, especially compound movements, than would be in a more advanced subject. For purposes of illustrating this point, let’s consider the

Chest Press exercise. In a novice subject, the Chest Press will stimulate (and therefore grow) the muscles of the chest, shoulders, and triceps. In an advanced subject the Chest Press will likely only grow one of those muscle groups because the others will have been fully developed to the extent they can by that movement. This is great news for beginners because they will get “more bang for their buck” on fewer movements. It also helps us with programming as we can cover more area with compound exercises (e.g. Big 5) and have a better chance of actually stimulating most of the muscles in the body. The other side of this is that advanced subjects will likely require more specific single joint exercises to ensure a stimulus.
Where to start:

During the consultation, the client will most likely be introduced to three exercises. These three exercises will become a core part of the client’s routine moving forward . Eventually they can be more strategically programmed to benefit an advanced trainee, but in the early stages we will build upon these movements:
1. Leg Press 2. Compound Row 3. Lumbar
How to evolve:

(Importantly, the following program is just an example meant to give an idea of how to view long term programming). Now, let’s look at what an optimal A/B routine might eventually evolve into and discuss some of the reasoning behind the exercises and placement chosen. Keep in mind this routine would be developed after a client has been with us for at least two months:
A routine B routine
ADD(f)/LC(m) ABD
SD(f)/CP(m) Pd
CR LC (f)/Flye(m)
TR/Abs LE
OH(f)/LR(m) SR
PO CP(f)/OH(m)
LP Lumb f = female; m = male

The first thing to note is that there are 7 exercises in each routine. While there is nothing inherently “magical” about that number, it has been consistently proven to be achievable by hundreds of MSF clients over the years.
‘Achievable’ here means that they can be completed in the allotted time and with the requisite intensity to ensure a stimulus. Remember, 20 minutes is the
MINIMUM time, not the standard. If we are to get consistent long-term results for our clients, most sessions will exceed the 20 minute mark.

The next thing we should point out here is that there are a few instances where specific ‘female’ exercises are programmed and specific ‘male’ exercises are programmed. This is simply based on the fact that over the years, these groups have generally requested certain areas of the body be targeted. For instance, females have generally requested more abdominal and hip work, whereas males have requested more chest, shoulders, and low back. At the end of the day, we don’t have to strictly adhere to these differentiations outlined above. In fact, it would be more advisable to refer to the specific request of each client. In this case, and for more examples please see the Exercise Selection Template document located here:
Academy - Programming and Progression 7 - Exercise Selection Template .

The most unique attribute of the A/B routines posted above is in the attempt to provide overlapping coverage of muscle regions, while also creating variety for the clients. For instance, in an effort to ensure that the entirety of the upper back muscles are trained in both sessions, the A routine includes the Compound Row (rear delt, traps, rhomboids, biceps) and Pullover (lats).
The B routine, then, includes the Simple Row (rear delt, traps, rhomboids) and

Pulldown (lats, biceps). Another example would be that of the muscles of the lower body. In the A routine, we rely on the Leg Press (quads, glutes, hips) and in the B routine we have programmed the Leg Extension (quads), Abduction (glutes, hips), and Lumbar (glutes, adductors).
Lumbar and Leg Press:

Also notice that the Lumbar and the Leg Press are eventually split and become part of two different workouts. It has been our experience that these two exercises are better when they are not performed in the same workout.

There tends to be some degree of “interference” in the lower back created during the Lumbar and then sensed during the Leg Press. This does not mean that these two exercises can never be performed in the same workout or that it is inherently dangerous. It is just that we can proactively prevent this from becoming an issue by performing Lumbar with Leg Extension instead of Leg

Press. So we will introduce the Lumbar and Leg Press together during the consult but then eventually split them up as the subject becomes stronger and more proficient at training intensely. However, if these two exercises are performed in the same workout then make sure to put as much space between them to minimize any overlapping lower back sensations. We should never perform these two exercises consecutively unless to use the
Lumbar as a much lighter, therapeutic modality.

At this point, one might wonder, “what is to be done with the other machines in the studio”? The answer to that is quite simple. Find any and every opportunity to use them to tailor the workout experience to the client. This is also where the Exercise Selection Template linked above will come into play. If for instance, we had a client that wanted to target their arms specifically, then using the Biceps Curl and/or Triceps Extension machines would be a priority.

These can easily be added on to the existing routines above if time permits or used to replace a lower priority muscle group. Just make sure that the arms, in this case, are being targeted in both workouts in keeping with the twice per week frequency requirement.

One last point to make here is that these routines should take at least 8 weeks (or 16 sessions) to fully build out. It is in our and the client’s best interest to slowly introduce these movements over time rather than all at once. There is a learning curve to our training methodology and the focus needs to be on the quality of the execution and tolerance of intensity. This is only complicated by constantly adding in new movement patterns. Plus, it creates an expectation of the client that exercise variety is somehow necessary. They will come to believe that the next new machine is “the one they’ve been missing”, when it is likely their execution and intensity that are holding them back. Remember, they will begin with an A routine that will take two to three weeks alone to begin to master before then gradually building out the B routine. The B routine should be established by replacing one complementary exercise of the A routine every week or so until the new routine has been completed in its entirety. Please reference the article entitled Exercise Selection and Long-Term Programming for more insight on how to progress various client types over time.

blocks.text: The following document can be used as a guideline when determining which exercises to incorporate for the Initial Consultation as well as when establishing an initial A and B routine for a variety of client types. In some situations, a client may come to us down the road with a new goal or concern, in which case we can begin to modify their routine accordingly.

The most sensible place to start will be the client’s intake form (demographics) where they will list any orthopedic issues or concerns they have along with any goals or target areas they would like to address. This form, in addition to the discussions we have with them during the consultation or in subsequent sessions will provide insight as to what movement patterns will be most beneficial. Keep in mind that from a very high level, a conservative approach would be to simply select one movement from each of the following five categories:
Upper Body - Upper Body - Lower Body Trunk/Spine/ Hips

Programming and/or sequencing to potentially avoid:

LE+LP - Leg Extension and Leg Press in the same session tends to be a lot of quadriceps stimulus. This should rarely be used for our clients especially those that are intensity adverse or in the older demographic.

These two exercises would be more beneficial on two non-consecutive days as we are ensuring a more frequent stimulus for the quads while allowing enough time for recovery. If we do decide to include in the same workout, make sure it is what the client needs and do not push to failure on both exercises (or either) when introducing. This should be discussed with the Studio Leader before implementing.

Lumb→LP - Performing Lumbar directly into Leg Press should be avoided as the fatigue from the lumbar exercise will invariably carry over into the leg press. Even when the lumbar is performed at a lower intensity. This can be an extremely uncomfortable feeling for the wrong reasons. The instructor may find the complementary pairing of Lumbar with Leg Extension (instead of LP) to be beneficial.

Lumb→LC - During a properly executed Leg Curl, there will be a tendency to extend the lower back, especially as effort increases. If we complete a set of Lumbar Extension immediately before the Leg Curl, the fatigue in the lower back will tend to make the extension required on the LC extremely uncomfortable. Especially for those subjects that are sensitive to spinal extension. For this reason, it may be better advised to program these two movements in separate workouts.
LP/LE→Lumb/Abs - Performing any quadriceps movement directly into

Lumbar can be quite uncomfortable on the quadriceps because of the pressure from the femur restraint mechanism. Additionally, the Lumbar requires a higher level of technical proficiency and control as a means of ensuring safety. When the lower body has been fatigued immediately beforehand, it makes the Lumbar exercise harder to accurately perform.

Pd→CR or CR→Pd - When two pulling movements are back to back in a workout, the gripping muscles will likely be the limiting factor. For many subjects, the gripping muscles are already a limiting factor with just one pulling movement. If the gripping muscles are extremely weak, we can be assured that they will adapt to grow stronger over time just as any other muscle will that is progressively challenged.

Lumb+Abs/Torso Rotation - Lumbar with Abdominals in the same workout can be problematic from the standpoint of the immediate effect of weakening of the core/trunk musculature. If one were to perform Lumbar first, the fatigue experienced in the low back would be present while performing the abdominal exercise. Since abdominals are ultimately trunk flexion, the low back is required to round/stretch, which can be uncomfortable after having been trained. Furthermore, the subject is likely to sense that the lower back is fatigued, which then becomes their point of focus. A similar consequence will be had if the

Abdominals are trained prior to the Lumbar muscles in the same workout. Having said all of this, it may still be beneficial in some situations to include both movements in the same workout. If a client is only training with us once per week and we wish to address both sets of muscles, it would be permissible to include both exercises. Additionally, there is a therapeutic effect that we can create training both movement patterns in the same workout. If this is the case, it seems through experience that performing the Abdominal exercise first with the Lumbar performed several exercises later is the best approach.

Basically, having fatigued abdominals going into Lumbar exercise is a more conservative approach then having fatigued lumbar muscles going into the Abdominal exercise. Additionally, both weights should be conservatively set and because this will be used as a more therapeutic approach, we are not looking for a high intensity effort. Use this approach with caution and involve your Studio Leader and/or MSF Corp to devise a strategy.

Any push→push or pull→pull - This is commonly known as a prefatigue in the strength training world. And while it has been popularized specifically by the high intensity faction, it is based on the faulty premise that fatigue is a stimulus for hypertrophy. Recall that mechanical tension is the only documented driver of hypertrophy and that importantly, only a recruited motor unit can experience tension. If we are training overlapping muscle groups (i.e. muscle fibers) back to back, there will undoubtedly be some fatigue present from the exercise before. This fatigue acts to reduce the motor unit recruitment (MUR) in the targeted muscle group(s) and as a result, the potential stimulus is diminished. Because of this, it is optimal to train non-overlapping muscles in consecutive sets. For instance, we would not want to perform a chest flye into the chest press, as the output possible in the chest press will be greatly reduced. Same with compound row into pulldown or leg extension into leg press. All of these pairings present the same problem; a reduction in MUR, which has negative consequences in terms of creating a stimulus.
Discussion on number of exercises

In the above examples you’ll notice that most of the workouts were constructed with 7 exercises. This should eventually be the average number of exercises in a session. Keep in mind that as MSF Exercise Practitioners, we want to provide a REMARKABLE experience for every client and every workout.
Part of that experience can be attributed to the fact that the workout should last at least 20 minutes and even longer than that in a majority of cases.

For a relatively new client, 5 exercises should likely take longer than 20 minutes for a couple of reasons. Firstly, we should be intentionally underestimating the strength of the new client in an effort to allow them to learn how to control their movement without being completely overwhelmed.

It should still be challenging as the set progresses, which would most likely land them at a 10 - 12 or more rep set. In addition to the higher number of reps contributing to a longer session, a new client will require the setup of each exercise along with more instruction and explanation. There will typically be discussions after each set too to reinforce the important concepts for our training protocol. Remember, we are teaching them an invaluable skill.

As a client progresses in their understanding and their level of strength, the instructor can challenge them with more load. As the load increases, the reps will decrease into the 6 to 10 range, which would be considered ideal for MOST (not all) clients. Along with that, they will require virtually no setup time and there will be limited instruction necessary as they will have been learning this whole time. As a result, the time per exercise will decrease, which will be more conducive to performing 6 to 8 exercises during the half hour time period.

topics.title: Considerations for Training with Pain
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/Considerations for Training with Pain.txt

blocks.text: When working with clients who have chronic pain attributable to either genetic reasons or overuse injuries, the first step is always to ask whether they have been formally diagnosed and what limitations, if any, their physician has recommended. This applies to conditions such as arthritis, tendonitis including golfer’s or tennis elbow, carpal tunnel syndrome, and similar issues.

While we cannot reverse these conditions, we can often improve comfort and tolerance by strengthening the muscles and joints surrounding the affected area. Careful strength training increases the capacity of the tissues to handle load, which can reduce irritation during daily activities. This is an area where
MaxStrength Fitness is uniquely effective, as our equipment allows us to train safely and precisely in ways that are often only available in a physical therapy setting.

Our main priority is always to assess tolerance. This means starting with very light resistance and possibly limiting the range of motion. If the client does not experience any increase in pain beyond what they normally feel, we can gradually add resistance and/or range of motion, and reassess. The goal is to find a level of load that is challenging but does not aggravate symptoms.
Because our machines can be progressed in two pound increments, we can make very small, precise increases as the client adapts and gets stronger.
The same can be done with the range of motion as well-small changes over time.

If the client is able to train with only limited use of the affected area, we may use most machines with either a static hold or timed static contraction (TSC) approach. As you’ll remember, a static hold involves holding an actual load in one position, usually near the midpoint in the range of motion. The TSC is a more conservative protocol where the subject will produce force against a static movement arm without holding a load. The movement arm is positioned in the desired location in the range of motion and then an excessive amount of weight is selected so that the movement arms cannot be moved. The subject is then instructed through three phases of increasing effort; 50%, 75%, and ending with an all out, 100% effort (or whatever can be comfortably sustained). Static execution allows us to strengthen the muscles around the joint without repeated movement that may irritate the area.

If the affected area happens to be the hands, wrists, or elbows and it is limiting to the point where we cannot train the upper body, we can work around it entirely while still delivering a productive workout. Hand pads are strongly recommended in these situations as they will blunt the pressure felt from the movement arm. If this is still too painful to endure, we may have to consider a “hands free” workout. With our full line of selectorized equipment, we can continue to train the major muscles of the shoulders and torso using machines such as the Lateral Raise, Simple Row, Pullover, and Chest Flye. All lower body and trunk machines remain fully available as well. This is an approach we have successfully used for many years.

The key point for clients to understand is that strength training does not have to worsen orthopedic conditions. When done carefully and intelligently, it can increase strength, improve joint support, and help clients feel more capable and confident in their daily lives. MaxStrength Fitness is well equipped to accommodate this and most other orthopedic concerns safely and effectively.

topics.title: Exercise Selection and Long-Term Programming
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/Exercise Selection and Long-Term Programming.txt

blocks.text: When deciding whether to add an exercise to a client’s program, the Exercise

Practitioner must evaluate several factors. The goal is not simply to increase the number of exercises performed, but to ensure that every addition improves the client’s results and experience without compromising the quality or intensity of the workout.
The following framework should guide the decision making process.
Key Questions Before Adding an Exercise 1. Will the addition improve or maintain the appropriate training frequency for the targeted muscles?
2. Will the exercise provide sufficient overlap in the muscle fibers being trained if different exercises are used between workouts?
3. Does the addition address a goal or concern expressed by the client, either verbally or through their intake information (demographics)?
4. Is there sufficient time/room available in the workout to perform the exercise with proper control and execution?
5. Can the client maintain the necessary intensity of effort if another exercise is added?
6. Will the addition improve the overall client experience without compromising training quality?

Each of these factors should be considered carefully before expanding a program. Keep in mind that most clients typically perform at least 6 exercises per workout (after the initial “learning curve” period of around 4 to 6 workouts). More advanced subjects might be able to perform 8 exercises or possibly more in a session. The points outlined below will help determine how to calibrate session volume on a client by client basis.
1. Training Frequency
A twice per week stimulus is necessary to optimize long term muscular adaptations.

Strength itself is not an adaptation but rather the outcome of a multitude of underlying adaptations, many of which are neurological. Because of this, strength can often be built or maintained with a once per week stimulus to that specific movement pattern.

Muscle growth, however, requires more consistent stimulation. Some hypertrophy will occur initially with a once per week workout, but progress will typically plateau soon after the base level adaptations are achieved.

Training once per week is still beneficial. Strength can be maintained and even improved with a high enough effort, and some muscle can be built or maintained. However, if the goal is to optimize muscular development and long-term progress, a twice per week stimulus is the more effective approach.

When deciding whether to add an exercise, the practitioner should consider whether the addition will help ensure that the targeted muscle groups (and more specifically, muscle fibers) are being stimulated twice per week.
2. Fiber Specific Adaptation and Exercise Overlap
Hypertrophy occurs within individual muscle fibers that experience sufficient mechanical tension.
If a muscle fiber is not recruited and exposed to meaningful mechanical tension, it will not benefit from the workout.

This principle has important implications for program design. Only the muscle fibers that are recruited in both workouts of the week will receive the necessary frequency of stimulation for optimal progress.
If certain hip muscles, for example, are stimulated in only one workout but not the second, the progress of those muscles will not reach full potential.
For this reason, performing the exact same exercises in both workouts is often the most reliable way to ensure that the same fibers are being trained consistently.

However, clients often prefer some variation in their programming. When variation is introduced, the practitioner must ensure that there is still substantial overlap in the muscle groups we wish to emphasize.

An example would be performing a pulldown in one workout and performing a pullover combined with a biceps curl in the other workout. In this case, the latissimus dorsi and biceps are still being trained in both sessions.

The key point is that if exercises differ between workouts, there must still be meaningful overlap in the muscle fibers being trained. And this becomes increasingly important as a subject becomes more advanced.
3. Client Feedback and Requests
Most clients will eventually express curiosity or interest in additional exercises or machines.

These requests may appear in several ways. A client may ask when they will be able to try other machines in the studio. They may express concern that a particular area of their body is not receiving enough attention. They may state, for instance, that they “feel their midsection needs more work”, or they may simply say that they would like to “do more machines”.

In these situations the Exercise Practitioner must be listening and ensure that the client feels heard. They should also be prepared to teach and inform and teach the client the fundamentals of resistance training including exercise selection and programming. The points made throughout this document and the entire MSF Academy are the considerations to be made for client education.

From the beginning of the client relationship, the practitioner should emphasize the importance of quality execution and effort rather than the number or variety of exercises performed. Clients should understand that results are driven by effort and mechanical tension applied to the muscles, not by the number of machines used during a workout. Importantly, the emphasis of quality over quantity is the primary attribute of the MSF protocol that helps to ensure the safety of each and every client.

At the same time, delivering a remarkable client experience is a priority. If a requested exercise can be added without compromising the quality or effectiveness of the workout, it is often appropriate to accommodate the request. Just expect that it will most likely have to become part of the routine moving forward in order to be effective and not just an occasional inclusion when requested.
The practitioner must balance education with responsiveness to the client’s interests.
4. Client Goals from the Demographics Packet
Exercise Practitioners should be very familiar with the information contained in the client’s demographics or intake form.

Clients frequently list goals such as strengthening the core, toning the arms, or improving overall strength. If a client takes the time to complete this form, it is important that the program clearly addresses the concerns they identified.
These goals should be discussed early in the client’s journey. The practitioner should explain which exercises in the program are intended to address those goals.

As discussed previously, targeted muscle groups should ideally be trained twice per week. In many cases this will mean performing the same exercise in both workouts in order to ensure consistent stimulation of the relevant muscle fibers.
Ensuring that client goals are clearly addressed in the exercise selection process can significantly improve client relationships and engagement.
5. Time Constraints Within the Workout
Every workout has a practical time limit.
When new clients begin training, the loads used are typically lighter in order to allow them to learn proper technique and develop control of the equipment.
Lighter loads generally lead to longer sets, often exceeding ten repetitions.
Because of this, sets tend to take longer to complete and the total number of exercises that can be performed within the workout is limited.
During this stage of training the primary focus should be on precise execution and exaggerated control of the load.

It is important to remember that twenty minutes is the MINIMUM amount of time for a workout, not the standard amount of time. Instructors should not rush or eliminate exercises in an effort to complete the workout sooner (i.e.
within 20 minutes).

As clients accumulate training experience they often become capable of producing the desired stimulus with heavier loads and fewer repetitions. As set durations shorten, additional exercises may become feasible within the available time.

This progression should be explained to clients early in their training experience. Practitioners should reinforce that quality execution is always the priority and that there may be opportunities to expand the program as the client becomes more advanced.

If a requested exercise can easily be added without compromising quality or time constraints, it may be appropriate to include it. However, the practitioner should not allow the program to be dictated entirely by the client’s desire to use more machines.
6. Intensity Limits Within the Workout
Just as every workout has a time limit, every workout should also have an intensity limit.

Advanced clients who train with precision and focus are capable of generating very high levels of effort. Because of this, there is a practical limit to the number of larger exercises (i.e. compound) that can be performed at the intensity required to create a meaningful stimulus.
Performing an additional exercise does not automatically lead to additional benefit. A certain level of intensity is required for an exercise to be productive.
There is an inverse relationship between intensity and volume. As the intensity of effort increases, the total amount of work that can be performed decreases.

For a highly focused and experienced client performing seven or eight exercises with appropriate intensity, it becomes increasingly unlikely that additional exercises can be added without reducing the quality of effort. This is where including more single joint movements can help. We are able to directly target specific muscle fibers/regions while creating less of a fatigue demand from larger movements.

While there may be occasional exceptions, the instructor should carefully observe the client’s effort level and remind them that their focus should be on getting more out of the exercises they are already performing rather than simply adding more exercises/volume.
As training experience increases, the importance of intensity of effort becomes even greater to insure a stimulus.
7. Establishing Authority and Building Trust
Exercise Practitioners should position themselves as knowledgeable authorities in strength training, but this authority must be earned through trust.
Trust is built through listening carefully to clients and approaching each interaction with genuine interest and empathy.
Practitioners should listen first and then look to inform/educate.

If a client raises a question that the practitioner cannot immediately answer, it is appropriate to acknowledge the question and indicate that further research or discussion with colleagues will be conducted. The instructor should then follow up with the client as soon as possible with a well informed response.

Additionally, the usefulness and insightfulness of the practitioner’s instruction goes a long way in establishing credibility with the clients. The MSF team should constantly strive to master their craft through reading, meetings, and discussion on various training topics. It is imperative in this profession that an instructor continue to stay engaged and add to their skill base.
This process strengthens trust and reinforces the professionalism of the MSF team.

When trust has been established, clients are more likely to accept guidance regarding the structure of their workouts, including decisions about whether additional exercises should or should not be included.

In some cases, a client may feel that a muscle group is not being addressed or that the workouts are “not challenging”. More often than not, the true issue is that the exercise is not being performed with enough intensity and/or proper technique. In these situations the solution will be improved execution rather than additional exercises and the practitioner must first be aware and then convincing enough to communicate this. Trust will only help the instructor in these situations.
Quality execution should always remain the priority.
Final Perspective
Every decision regarding exercise selection should support two goals. The first is delivering the most efficient, effective, and safe training stimulus possible.
The second is providing a remarkable experience for every client during every workout.
Adding an exercise to a program is often the easiest decision to make.
However, this should only occur after careful consideration of the factors outlined above.
Exercise Practitioners are not simply pushing clients through workouts. They are teaching a skill that can significantly influence long term health and physical capability.
Because of this, the practitioner must demonstrate attention to detail, thoughtful program design, and a clear commitment to the client’s success.

When this approach is consistently applied, clients begin to recognize that the practitioner cares more about the workout than they do. Over time this perspective helps shift the client’s focus away from quantity and toward the quality of effort and execution that ultimately drives progress.

topics.title: FAQ
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 6 - General Recommendations for Programming and Progression/FAQ.txt

blocks.text: The short answer…? You will end up at the same place if you are training to or at least near failure, so from a high level perspective, it does not matter. But here's what does matter:
Higher Reps (approx 10 plus) create a higher level of perceived effort through:
More reps = more fatigue
Increased cardiovascular demand
Increased afferent feedback (discomfort, lactic acid, "burn")
Longer duration, more mentally taxing

Perceived effort limits the level of motor unit recruitment that can be achieved in any maximal effort contraction. Simply stated, the more we "feel" any discomfort, the fewer muscle fibers we will be able to activate/recruit/use. This is known as the maximum level of tolerable effort...we just can't tolerate any more. And this likely happens well before we get the required stimulus we seek from training (mechanical tension).

So this would lead us to believe that heavier weight and fewer reps are superior. The problem with this approach is that most people are not capable of handling a "heavier" weight that brings them to failure in 5 to 7 reps. They don't have the ability to control that amount of load and they require more "practice" with lighter loads and higher reps.

Usually with newer clients, we will automatically default to lighter weights for purposes of learning all of the qualitative elements we require (posture, pace, path) and particularly the lower turnarounds. Over time, we begin to increase the loads and their reps should come down, but only to the extent that they maintain their form. Oftentimes we'll reach a point where the client begins to wrestle the weight rather than use it with control. We need to constantly remind them that there is a standard of quality to maintain. But if I have a client that is compliant and follows instruction, I will absolutely try and progress them to a lower rep range.
Am I getting stronger?

Aside from asking “was that more weight?” asking “am I getting stronger?” seems to be one of the more frequently asked questions. And while we could simply answer yes or no…they would most likely require further explanation to satisfy them. With this being the case, a little background information is necessary for perspective.

Firstly, anyone engaging in a properly designed, safely performed, progressively challenged strength training program can expect to get stronger. This is especially true for those that haven't done any sort of strength training in the recent past. So most assuredly we can answer “yes” to that inquiry. But the reason they are asking must be because they are unaware themselves or need to be convinced. This is an unfortunate occurrence.

It could be that the person asking lives a relatively inactive life, in which case they would not have an opportunity to notice or prove to themselves that they have in fact gotten stronger. Again, this is unfortunate but probably not that uncommon. But if this is the case, then any amount of strength training done with any level of intensity should represent a profound “wake up call” of sorts.

Or it could be that this particular individual is just physically unaware of themselves, which would tend to be the case for a good number of our clients as that is what possibly drew them to MSF in the first place. In other words, they don’t know how to tell or measure their new levels of strength and want an objective measurement from the workout chart. While the answer would be, “yes, you are lifting more weight than you did when you started,” that can be a little misleading.

It can almost be guaranteed that one will go on to lift more weight at MSF than when they first joined. Part of the reason is because we will start conservatively with them, using significantly lighter weights than they are currently capable of lifting to facilitate the learning process. It takes time and attention to learn how to properly strength train and our focus is always on the qualitative approach. So the relative light weights that we start with will soon be surpassed as the client learns how to control their movement and effort. In this case, it is likely that they have gotten stronger as the neurological adaptations alone that take place very quickly, on a rep-to-rep basis at times, are a big component of getting stronger. On a side note, strength itself is not an adaptation, but rather an outcome. There are 6 or more adaptations that go into making someone stronger of which neurological efficiency and muscle mass are two of the major ones.

Now in the case of an advanced client that has been training for 3 - 5 years or more, there is a chance that they have reached their genetic “ceiling” in terms of strength. In fact everyone is likely to reach this point if they subject themselves to enough stimulus (i.e. training sessions). But once we reach this point, it would make zero sense to stop training as we would then begin to lose our strength. So it’s best to just keep training without concern for a genetic limit. Just assume that it doesn’t even exist, keep training, and at least maintain as much strength as you can for the rest of your life.

All of that to say that the real bottleneck in all of this usually comes down to the willingness or tolerance of the client to produce a truly hard and adaptive effort. When someone first begins a strength training program (or any physical activity for that matter), almost everything will be stimulative as it will be at a level above what they are currently used to. However, as one gets stronger, the current level of effort will not be enough to surpass the newfound level of strength. A harder, more intense effort is required to keep progressing.

This is a simple biological adaptation model. The more someone has engaged in training, the higher the level of output is required to be stimulative. But the good news is, with more training comes more ability and tolerance and skill. The subject should be capable of training harder because of the practice of training and the instruction they receive. This is the primary purpose of an Exercise Practitioner. Aside from ensuring their safety of course.

There should be no doubt to the subject that they themselves have gotten stronger if they are consistently training with us and they are focused on their intensity and technique. They should be able to feel the difference proper strength training makes by just standing there with an awareness. If not and we need to point to other examples, we have gotten plenty of input over the years:
Posture
Less joint pain
Getting out of bed
Up and down stairs
Getting in and out of the car
Golfing
Carrying groceries
Lifting up children
Yardwork
Opening doors
Walking through stores or the neighborhood
Loading/unloading items from the trunk
Getting off the floor
Getting out of a chair
Lifting suitcase into overhead storage

All of these would be indicative of an increase in strength. They are all also improved with practice as any physical endeavor is specific. If one wants to get better at going up and down stairs or getting off the floor, these should be carefully practiced. The strength increase will make all of those things easier but the point being that there is also a skill component.

So to sum up, yes, everyone that begins training with us will assuredly become stronger. The question is, how much and to what degree? And this is entirely up to the individual. How seriously will they take their sessions and the instruction? How much will they challenge themselves to get better at strength training? The Instructor will not hold them back and they will even encourage, but ultimately it is up to the client to decide how hard they want to work over time. In this way, they will not ever have to question whether they are getting stronger, they will give their body no choice.
I don’t want to get “bulky” ( I just want to get more “toned”)
The muscular response to resistance training is genetically mediated and it cannot be changed.
Osteoporosis, Osteopenia, and Bone Density Concerns
Is strength training safe if I have osteoporosis or osteopenia?
Yes, when it is done correctly and under proper supervision. At MaxStrength
Fitness, exercises are controlled, customized to your abilities, and progressed gradually. This allows your muscles and bones to adapt safely without unnecessary strain.
Can strength training actually improve bone density?

Strength training can help slow bone loss and, in many cases, improve bone density. When muscles work against resistance, they pull on bones and signal the body to maintain or build stronger bone tissue. This type of effort is especially important for bone health. Additionally, high-intensity strength training encourages the release of chemical messengers in the body known as myokines that signal the creation of bone tissue.
Will lifting weights increase my risk of fractures?

Our Continuous Tension protocol and supervision ensure that the strength training is performed safely and avoids excessive or sudden loading during exercise. Properly performed strength training reduces fracture risk over time.
Stronger muscles support and protect your bones, improve joint stability, and lower the risk of falls, which is the most common cause of fractures in people with low bone density.
What if I already have joint pain or past injuries?
Exercises are always adjusted to your comfort level and medical history.
Machines, ranges of motion, and resistance levels are selected specifically to avoid painful or unsafe positions while still providing benefit.
Do I need to lift heavy weights for bone health?
You need enough resistance to challenge your muscles, but “heavy” is relative and always individualized. The goal is meaningful effort with precision control, not lifting maximal weights.
How long does it take to see benefits?

Improvements in strength, balance, and confidence often occur within a few sessions. Changes in bone density take longer to physiologically manifest and require consistency, but every workout contributes to protecting your long-term bone health.
Why not just do walking or light exercise?

Walking is excellent for overall health, but it does not provide enough stimulus to meaningfully strengthen bones. Strength training applies the kind of external resistance bones need to adapt and stay strong.
What makes MaxStrength Fitness different?
Our training focuses on slow, controlled movement, individualized resistance, and focused supervision. This allows us to safely work with clients who may not be comfortable with traditional gyms.
